answers.about: What you pay the Town, why it changed, and what it is not.
answers.q: Why did my property taxes go up this year?
answers.a: The Town's total town-wide rate rose from $67.031 to $71.598 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2026 — an increase of 6.81%.

answers.about: What you pay the Town, why it changed, and what it is not.
answers.q: How much more am I actually paying?
answers.a: On a home assessed at $37,200 — roughly $500,000 of market value at the Town's 7.44% residential ratio — the Town's share went from about $2,493.55 to $2,663.45. That is roughly $169.89 more for the year.

answers.about: What you pay the Town, why it changed, and what it is not.
answers.q: Where does the Town portion of my tax money go?
answers.a: Of the $71.598 rate, $61.948 is the General Fund, $8.695 the Highway Fund and $0.955 street lighting.

answers.about: What you pay the Town, why it changed, and what it is not.
answers.q: Is this my whole tax bill?
answers.a: No — and this is the single most common misreading. Everything on this site covers the TOWN portion only. School, county, fire district and library taxes are levied by separate governments and billed separately; for most Riverhead households the school portion is the largest line on the bill.

answers.about: The size of the budget, what dominates it, and what moved.
answers.q: How much does Riverhead spend in a year?
answers.a: $121,110,904 adopted for 2026 across all 19 operating funds. The General Fund — the one most Town services run through — is $69,113,159 of that.

answers.about: The size of the budget, what dominates it, and what moved.
answers.q: What does the Town actually spend the most on?
answers.a: Police and people. Public safety is 35.8% of the 2026 General Fund ($24,761,480) and employee benefits and debt another 36.9% ($25,507,319) — together 72.7% before a single other service is funded.

answers.about: The size of the budget, what dominates it, and what moved.
answers.q: What changed from last year?
answers.a: Compare any two budget years line by line — by fund, by department, or by individual account — and sort by what moved most.

answers.topic: Who works here and what they earn
answers.about: Headcount, pay, overtime — the published payroll, not estimates.
answers.q: How many people work for the Town, and what does that cost?
answers.a: 574 people appeared on the 2025 payroll, for $37,982,278 in gross pay — up from $36,929,954 in 2024.

answers.topic: Who works here and what they earn
answers.about: Headcount, pay, overtime — the published payroll, not estimates.
answers.q: Who is the highest-paid Town employee?
answers.a: In 2025 it was Patrick O McDermott (Detective Sergeant) at $380,613 gross. Gross pay includes overtime, longevity and any payout of accrued time — it is not a base salary.

answers.topic: Who works here and what they earn
answers.about: Headcount, pay, overtime — the published payroll, not estimates.
answers.q: What does a typical Town employee earn?
answers.a: The median 2025 gross was $56,391, against an average of $66,171. The gap between the two is the tell: a handful of very large packages pull the average well above what most employees actually earn.

answers.topic: Who works here and what they earn

answers.about: What the Town owes, what it owes it for, and what it costs to carry.
answers.q: How much does Riverhead owe?
answers.a: $38,423,858 in bonded debt as of December 31, 2025, plus $21,975,000 in outstanding bond anticipation notes.

answers.about: What the Town owes, what it owes it for, and what it costs to carry.
answers.q: What is a BAN, and why should I care?
answers.a: A bond anticipation note is short-term borrowing — the Town takes the money now and decides later whether to pay it off or convert it into long-term bonds. Riverhead is carrying $21,975,000 of them, so the decision to bond or repay is a real one with real cost either way.

answers.about: What the Town owes, what it owes it for, and what it costs to carry.
answers.q: What is the Town's credit rating?
answers.a: Aa2 from Moody's Investors Service, affirmed February 16, 2024. Rating matters because it sets what the Town pays to borrow.

answers.topic: Is the Town in good shape?
answers.about: Savings (the fund balance), the cushion, and whether the position is improving.
answers.q: Does the Town have savings?
answers.a: $28,829,513 in unassigned General Fund balance at the end of 2025, as audited — 41.7% of appropriations, against the 15% floor in the Town's fund balance policy (Resolution 918 of 2011), which sets no ceiling.

answers.topic: Is the Town in good shape?
answers.about: Savings (the fund balance), the cushion, and whether the position is improving.
answers.q: Is holding that much savings good or bad?
answers.a: Both readings are legitimate and the page gives you each. A large cushion protects the credit rating and absorbs a bad year; it is also money collected from taxpayers and not spent, sitting at 2.8 times the floor in the Town's own policy — which lists cutting the next year's property taxes as one use for money above it.

answers.about: The 2027 budget: the projection, the choices, and the deadline.
answers.q: Will my taxes go up again in 2027?
answers.a: The Town's 2027 Tentative Budget is out. It proposes a town-wide tax levy of $62,882,202, up 2.79% from 2026, for the General Fund, Highway and Street Lighting. With the special districts, the levy is $67,159,863, up 2.78% from 2026 and $1,807,211 less than this site’s forecast of $68,967,074. The Supervisor’s letter says every taxing district is within the tax cap limit of 2.79%, and no district’s levy rises by more than that. It is a proposal: the Board can change it before adopting a budget by November 20.

answers.about: The 2027 budget: the projection, the choices, and the deadline.
answers.q: What are the Town Board's options for my 2027 taxes?
answers.a: There are 5: hold the levy flat, cut it, raise it inside the cap, raise it above the cap, or a hybrid of savings and reserves. Each has a levy number, a dollar amount the Board would have to find, and a different legal requirement — only going above the cap needs an override vote.

answers.about: The 2027 budget: the projection, the choices, and the deadline.
answers.q: Could Riverhead just freeze taxes, like Suffolk County did?
answers.a: It is arithmetically possible and harder than it sounds. A flat levy has to absorb $3,514,315 of projected General Fund cost growth, and unlike Suffolk, Riverhead's police department sits inside the very fund a freeze would apply to. The 2027 Tentative raises the General Fund levy by $1,472,341, so that is what a freeze would now have to find.

answers.about: The 2027 budget: the projection, the choices, and the deadline.
answers.q: When does the Board actually decide, and can I say anything?
answers.a: The 2027 Tentative is out, so the Board’s part has begun. The Supervisor files a tentative budget by September 30. The public hearing falls on or before the Thursday after the November election, and the Board must adopt by November 20. The hearing is the formal moment residents are heard.

answers.about: Who decides, how they voted, and who funds them.
answers.q: Did the Town Board vote for this?
answers.a: Resolutions are indexed with how each member voted, and the ones carrying a dollar figure are tagged with it.

answers.about: Who decides, how they voted, and who funds them.
answers.q: Who represents me, and what are they responsible for?
answers.a: The Supervisor prepares the budget; the Council adopts it. Both are on the record here, with the statutory qualifications for each office.

answers.about: Who decides, how they voted, and who funds them.
answers.q: Who is funding their campaigns?
answers.a: Filings come live from the New York State Board of Elections, including contributions from people who also appear on the Town payroll.

answers.about: Who decides, how they voted, and who funds them.
answers.q: What is the Town Square project costing taxpayers?
answers.a: The land sale, the credits against it, what the Town pays the developer, the parking arrangement and the votes that authorized each piece — read from the master developer agreement itself, not from coverage of it.

limits.q: What is my actual tax bill?
limits.a: This site estimates the TOWN portion from the Town's own published rate table. It does not know your parcel. For the real bill — every jurisdiction, amounts due and payment status — use the Town's official lookup.

limits.q: When is my payment due, and where do I pay it?
limits.a: Due dates, penalty schedule and payment methods are set by the Receiver of Taxes, not by anything published here.

limits.q: Why is my school tax so high?
limits.a: School districts are separate governments with their own budgets, their own boards and their own public votes. They are the largest part of most Riverhead tax bills and none of it is Town money. Nothing on this site covers them.

limits.q: What is my assessed value, and can I challenge it?
limits.a: Assessment is set by the Town Assessor on the annual roll. This site takes assessed value as an input — it neither sets nor holds it — and grievance is a separate statutory process with its own deadline.

limits.q: Why does a particular employee earn what they earn?
limits.a: The payroll here shows what was paid. It does not show why — the contract step, the assignment, the accrued time paid out. Gross pay is a fact; the explanation behind any individual figure is not something this data contains.
